On the flat's balcony one evening, over tea:
Varun: I have to confess something embarrassing.
Lalremsiami: Uh-oh.
Varun: Before I moved here, my aunt warned me about people from your state. She said you all keep to yourselves and don't mix.
Lalremsiami: And then you met me, the loudest person on the floor.
Varun: And the person who lent me a cooker and stayed up helping me with my resume.
Lalremsiami: I still don't know your aunt.
Varun: I told her about you, actually. She wants to meet you at Diwali.
Lalremsiami: Bring her. I'll make her cook something with me.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami lend Varun?
qa.a: Lalremsiami lent Varun a cooker.

qa.q: How does Varun feel about repeating the warning, and what shows it?
qa.a: Embarrassed but honest; Varun calls it a confession and follows it with kind examples of Lalremsiami.

qa.q: What did Varun do that let personal contact replace the warning?
qa.a: Varun told the aunt about Lalremsiami, and now the aunt wants to meet Lalremsiami at Diwali.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt hearing the warning?
qa.a: Amused but perhaps a little stung, since the reply teases first; the offer to cook with the aunt shows openness.

grounding: A young adult makes a friendship across a divide they were warned about and tells the stories at home.

passage: Growing up I was told never to go past the canal, because the colony on the other side was "not our kind". I never asked who had said it. At twenty-four I started at a design firm, and my desk-mate was Pranav, who lived in exactly that colony. He brought jaggery sweets on his birthday and drew a map of his lane for me on a napkin. I went one Sunday, and Pranav's mother scolded me for being thin and fed me twice. I came home and told my family about the fish curry and the cricket in the lane. My grandfather said nothing for a moment, then asked, "Is that where the good chai is?" I said yes. He nodded slowly. Sonali

qa.q: What did Pranav draw for Sonali on a napkin?
qa.a: Pranav drew a map of his lane on a napkin.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about the warning, and how did that change?
qa.a: The warning had gone unquestioned, but after the visit Sonali felt welcomed and fed, and the old idea seemed doubtful.

qa.q: What choice by Sonali helped break the old prejudice?
qa.a: Accepting Pranav's invitation and telling the stories at home.

qa.q: How might Sonali's grandfather have felt on hearing about the colony?
qa.a: Surprised and thoughtful, and a little curious; asking about the chai shows the old warning softening.

grounding: A young adult makes real friendships with people from a group they were warned about and tells the stories.

passage:
Coordinator's note, weekend literacy programme, Shanti Nagar community centre.
When Abhinav joined us as a volunteer in March, he told me his family had warned him: "Don't go into that basti, those people will rob you." He came anyway, clutching his bag the first week. He was paired with Jeevan, who grew up in the basti and runs our evening maths class. For a while they only talked about lesson plans. Then Jeevan's mother fed him poha, and Abhinav came back the next week with his own mother's laddoos.
Now they plan together every Saturday. Jeevan helped Abhinav fix his bike; Abhinav helped Jeevan with a scholarship form. Last week I heard Abhinav telling a new volunteer, "My parents were scared of this place. Then they met Jeevan at my birthday. Now my father asks about his exams." I think the stories he tells at home are doing as much as our classes.

qa.q: What did Jeevan's mother feed Abhinav?
qa.a: Poha.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel in his first week at the centre, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt nervous and wary, clutching his bag, because his family had warned him about the basti.

qa.q: What helped Abhinav's family change their view?
qa.a: Abhinav's real friendship with Jeevan, and meeting Jeevan at the birthday, gave them a person to know instead of a warning to believe.

qa.q: How might Jeevan experience Abhinav's changing attitude?
qa.a: Jeevan probably feels respected and trusted, seen as a friend and colleague rather than as someone from a feared place.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who makes a real friendship across a divide he was warned about, and tells the story at home.

passage:
Wednesday night, Raipur
Six months since I moved in with Minakshi, and I finally told Mama the whole story on the phone today. Before I came, every aunty warned me: "Those tribal district people drink, they're backward, keep your door locked." My own mother made me promise to change flats if anything felt wrong.
What actually happened: Minakshi nursed me through dengue in July. She taught me to make bamboo shoot pickle. She reads more books than anyone I know and is two years from being a forest officer. Her little brother calls me didi on the phone.
Mama went quiet, then said, "We didn't know anyone from there." I said, "Now you know one." She asked if Minakshi would come for Diwali. I cried a little after the call. Relief, I think, and something like shame for what I used to believe.
Kalyani

qa.q: What did Minakshi teach Kalyani to make?
qa.a: Bamboo shoot pickle.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel after the phone call with Mama?
qa.a: Kalyani felt relieved and a little ashamed, and cried a little after the call.

qa.q: What made Mama's view start to change?
qa.a: Hearing real stories about Minakshi, who nursed Kalyani and is studying to be a forest officer, gave Mama an actual person to know.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel if she heard about the aunties' warnings?
qa.a: She might feel hurt at being called backward, and warmed that Kalyani's friendship is changing the family's view.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who forms a real friendship with someone from a group she was warned about and tells the story to her family.

passage: When the highway crew put up tin sheds outside Pimpalgaon, Akash's uncle locked the tractor shed twice. "Outsiders," he said. "Keep the goats in." But Akash, home after his farming diploma, needed the water pump fixed, and the only mechanic within ten kilometres was Harsha from the camp. Harsha fixed it in an hour and waved away the chai money, saying his father had grown ragi back in Karnataka until the rains failed. They started meeting at the tea stall after work. Harsha taught Akash to read the wind before spraying; Akash helped him fill in a form for his daughter's school. At dinner, Akash began telling the stories: Harsha's daughter topping her class, Harsha pulling a boy out of the canal. His uncle only grunted at first. Then one Sunday he packed a tiffin of bhakri and walked it over to the camp himself.

qa.q: What did Harsha teach Akash?
qa.a: Harsha taught Akash to read the wind before spraying.

qa.q: What does Akash's habit of telling the stories at dinner suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He is fond of his new friend and hopeful his family will see Harsha as a person, so he keeps telling the stories even when his uncle only grunts.

qa.q: Which of Akash's choices did most to soften his uncle, and why?
qa.a: Sharing real stories at dinner, because details like the daughter topping her class and the canal rescue replaced the word "outsiders" with a real neighbour.

qa.q: How has Akash's uncle's view changed by the end?
qa.a: He moves from locking the shed and calling the crew outsiders to carrying bhakri to the camp himself, a sign his suspicion has eased.

grounding: Shows a young adult forming a real friendship with a worker from a group he was warned about and telling the stories, which softens an uncle's prejudice.
